answerKey.primaryProblem: Uncontrolled Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus with concurrent HFrEF (EF 40%), CKD stage 3, and dietary nonadherence driven by psychosocial barriers and inconsistent medication adherence
differential: Food/nutrition-related knowledge deficit regarding sodium and carbohydrate intake
Inconsistent medication intake contributing to poor glycemic and volume control (not a true 'diet-only' problem)
Unintentional weight loss possibly reflecting cardiac cachexia/early sarcopenia versus inadequate intake versus fluid shifts from diuretic changes
Depression/social isolation contributing to poor self-care (consider screening/referral)
keyFindings: HbA1c 8.7% and fasting glucose 165 mg/dL indicate poor glycemic control
Creatinine 1.6 mg/dL and BUN 28 mg/dL indicate CKD stage 3, relevant for protein/sodium/potassium planning and NSAID avoidance
Sodium intake pattern (canned soups, restaurant food, no water) inconsistent with HF/CKD-appropriate sodium restriction
Unintentional 10 lb (4.8%) weight loss in one month is clinically significant and needs further workup, not simply 'good news' for a diabetic/overweight patient
Pharmacy refill pattern suggests inconsistent metformin and eplerenone adherence despite patient believing he 'mostly' takes his pills
Frequent NSAID (ibuprofen) use is a a risk factor for worsening renal function and fluid retention in HF/CKD and is not currently recognized by the patient as relevant to his heart/kidney condition
Patient is in precontemplation/early contemplation stage of readiness to change dietary habits
plan: Establish rapport and use motivational interviewing to explore ambivalence rather than prescribing a rigid diet

Collaboratively develop a PES statement, e.g., 'Excessive sodium and inadequate fiber/fluid-pattern intake related to limited health literacy regarding heart failure/diabetes interaction and social eating patterns as evidenced by elevated HbA1c, BP 158/92, and reported high-sodium convenience/restaurant food intake'
Negotiate small, patient-chosen behavior changes (e.g., one lower-sodium swap at dinner club, water alternating with soda) rather than wholesale diet overhaul
Address unintentional weight loss: discuss with medical team, consider malnutrition/cardiac cachexia workup, avoid recommending caloric restriction until clarified
Coordinate with prescriber regarding metformin GI side effects (consider extended-release formulation) and reinforce importance of eplerenone for HF without inducing fear of hypotension

Educate on connection between sodium intake, fluid retention, blood pressure, and heart failure symptoms in plain language, correcting the belief that diabetes and heart failure are 'the same sick thing'
Discuss risks of frequent NSAID (ibuprofen) use in the context of CKD and HF; suggest discussing alternative pain management with his physician

Identify community resources: home-delivered meals, diabetes self-management education, social work for financial/food insecurity, consider referral to cardiology/nephrology care coordination and physical therapy for safe activity
Set a collaborative, patient-owned short-term goal and schedule follow-up to reassess readiness and barriers
redFlags: Unintentional weight loss of 4.8% body weight in 1 month warrants prompt communication with the medical team
Low-normal sodium (136) combined with HF and possible medication nonadherence requires monitoring for worsening heart failure/hyponatremia
Frequent NSAID use in a patient with CKD stage 3 and HF is a safety concern requiring provider follow-up
Pattern of nonadherence to metformin/eplerenone noted in refill history should be communicated to the care team, not just addressed with diet
educationPoints: Heart failure and diabetes are related but distinct conditions; sodium primarily affects fluid balance/heart failure while carbohydrate intake primarily affects blood glucose
Low-sodium does not have to mean low-flavor; herbs, spices, acid (vinegar/citrus), and aromatics can replace salt
Reading restaurant menus and asking for modifications (sauce on the side, no added salt) can allow him to keep eating with his dinner club
Water or unsweetened options can help with thirst without worsening blood glucose, versus sugary soda/fruit punch
Routine use of ibuprofen can be harmful to kidneys and worsen fluid retention in heart failure; safer pain options should be discussed with his physician
Unintentional weight loss, even in someone who is overweight, is a signal that needs medical attention, not necessarily a 'win'

Taking medications consistently, even when side effects are bothersome, is important; side effects (like metformin nausea) are often manageable with simple changes (timing, formulation) rather than skipping doses

artifacts.body: 72 y/o male with HFrEF, EF 40% on last echo, s/p CABG 5 years ago, CAD, HTN, CKD stage 3. Reports fatigue and exertional dyspnea, grade 2/4 on exertion. Exam: apical systolic murmur, bilateral basilar crackles, 2+ bilateral pedal edema, 3+ peripheral pulses, skin warm and dry with delayed venous filling. Continue lisinopril and eplerenone. History of 2 HF-related hospitalizations in the past 12 months. Counseled on sodium restriction and daily weights; patient states he understands but has had difficulty adhering. Will follow up in 3 months or sooner if symptoms worsen.

facts.chart: Patient states he was sent by his PCP for diet counseling related to diabetes and heart failure.
facts.says: Doc sent me here. Said I need to talk to somebody about my eating. I don't really see the point, but here I am.

facts.chart: Reports metformin causes nausea/vomiting.
facts.says: Those pills, man. The metformin one, it makes me feel like I'm gonna throw up half the time.

facts.chart: Patient expresses skepticism about being referred to nutrition clinic and about student's experience.
facts.says: Do I need to fill out a form for this diet thing? You look like you're still in school. No offense.

facts.chart: Eats out twice weekly with a social dinner club at a chain restaurant with high-sodium, fried menu items.
facts.says: Me and my buddies go to the same place twice a week. Been going there for years. It's the one thing I look forward to.

facts.chart: Takes ibuprofen 400mg 2-3 times weekly for back pain; unaware of renal/cardiac risk.
facts.says: My back gets stiff, so I pop a couple Advil, maybe 2 or 3 times a week. Why, is that a problem?

facts.chart: Believes diabetes and heart failure are the same condition ('my sick thing').
facts.says: It's all the same sick thing to me, the sugar and the heart. Same difference, ain't it?

facts.chart: Drinks soda/sweet tea with meals, avoids plain water.
facts.says: Water's boring. I like my soda or sweet tea with my food. Makes it taste right.

facts.chart: Skips breakfast most days; largest meal at lunch; evening snacking.
facts.says: Breakfast? I don't really bother most days. Lunch is my big meal, then I pick at stuff at night.

facts.chart: Relies on canned soups, instant mac and cheese, and leftovers for home meals due to lack of cooking support.
facts.says: When I'm home alone I just open a can of soup or make that instant mac and cheese. Easy, and it tastes good too.

facts.chart: Reports difficulty getting up and getting to the grocery store due to fatigue.
facts.says: Mornings are rough. By the time I get moving, going to the store feels like a whole project.

facts.chart: Expresses guilt about not taking care of himself in relation to his sister living far away.
facts.says: My sister calls and worries. Makes me feel bad, like I'm letting her down by not taking care of myself.

facts.chart: Believes 'healthy eating' is for younger, wealthier, healthier people; views food as comfort and joy.
facts.says: That healthy eating stuff is for young folks with money. Food's supposed to make you feel good, not be a chore.

facts.chart: Expresses distrust that doctors/hospitals are motivated by profit from his repeated admissions.
facts.says: Sometimes I think they just want me back in that hospital bed so they can bill somebody.

facts.chart: Feels he failed as a husband/father by not following his diet in the past, fears being seen as a 'bad' person.
facts.says: My wife used to beg me to eat right. I didn't listen. Feel like I let her down, let my kids down too.

facts.chart: Was a janitor for decades; expresses fear and uncertainty about his health future.
facts.says: Thirty-some years mopping floors and fixing stuff. Now my own body's falling apart and I don't know what's next.

facts.chart: Has notable savings in checking account but avoids spending it, fearing waste.
facts.says: I got some money put away. I just... I don't like touching it. Feels like it's for something, I just don't know what.

facts.chart: States primary goal is avoiding re-hospitalization.
facts.says: I don't want to go back to that hospital. That's really all I care about at the end of the day.

facts.chart: States strong desire to maintain independence and not be treated as incapable.
facts.says: I don't need somebody telling me what to do like I'm a kid. I can still take care of myself.

facts.chart: Fears becoming a burden to his sister or friends.
facts.says: I don't want to be some burden my sister's gotta fly out here and deal with. That scares me more than anything.

facts.chart: Reports unintentional 10 lb weight loss over past month despite not actively dieting.
facts.says: I've been losing weight without trying. Ten pounds, maybe. I didn't do anything different.

facts.chart: Reports bilateral ankle swelling, worse by end of day.
facts.says: My ankles puff up something awful by the end of the day. Shoes don't even fit right by evening.

facts.chart: Reports shortness of breath with minimal exertion.
facts.says: I get winded just walking to the mailbox and back. Didn't used to be like that.

facts.chart: Reports nocturia multiple times nightly disrupting sleep, consistent with polyuria from hyperglycemia.
facts.says: I'm up two, three times a night to pee. Can't hardly get a decent night's sleep anymore.

facts.chart: Reports taking most medications daily but acknowledges sometimes forgetting the water pill (eplerenone).
facts.says: I take my pills pretty much every day. Maybe I forget the water pill sometimes, but mostly I'm good about it.

facts.chart: Drinks 1-2 small cups of beer nightly while watching TV; denies tobacco use ever.
facts.says: I'll have a beer or two, small ones, when I'm watching my shows at night. Never smoked a day in my life though.

facts.chart: States mother had diabetes; father died of heart disease.
facts.says: My mama had the sugar too. My daddy, he went from his heart, years back.

facts.chart: Dislikes bitter vegetables; prefers heavier, saucier dishes.
facts.says: Don't give me any of that bitter kale or whatever. I like my greens cooked down with some meat in there.

facts.chart: History of being physically active (walking, odd jobs) before heart failure; now frustrated by limitations.
facts.says: I used to be up and moving all day on my job. Now I can barely do a lap around the block. Makes me so mad.

facts.chart: Expresses ambivalence: acknowledges he should eat better but questions the point; also states he doesn't want to 'die on the couch.'
facts.says: I know I should eat better, but who's it gonna help at this point? ...But I also don't wanna just die sitting on this couch.

facts.chart: Widowed; no current partner.
facts.says: My wife passed a few years back. Been on my own since.

facts.chart: Has online/phone contact with retired friends via Facebook and email, but no in-person local support besides neighbors he doesn't interact with.
facts.says: I talk to some old work buddies on Facebook and email, keeps me company. But round here, I don't really bother with the neighbors.

facts.chart: Reports trying to eat 'less' on his own without professional guidance, with poor results and ongoing weight loss.
facts.says: I been trying to just eat less on my own. Doesn't seem to be doing much good though, 'cept I'm losing weight I didn't want to lose.

facts.chart: Reports soreness and stiffness in joints, treated with OTC ibuprofen.
facts.says: My joints get sore and stiff, especially my back. That's why I take the Advil.

facts.chart: Reports occasional bleeding gums when brushing; mild gum disease noted on exam.
facts.says: My gums bleed sometimes when I brush. Didn't think much of it.

mismatches.patientClaim: Walter states he takes his pills 'pretty much every day' and only occasionally forgets the water pill (eplerenone).
mismatches.recordEvidence: Pharmacy refill history shows metformin refilled every ~46 days and eplerenone every ~44 days on average over the past 6 months, both well beyond the expected 30-day interval, suggesting doses are being missed much more often than he reports.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Self-reported adherence often overestimates actual medication-taking behavior; triangulating patient report with objective data like refill history helps the dietitian understand true barriers (e.g., GI side effects, cost, forgetfulness) and tailor counseling and interprofessional referral appropriately rather than taking self-report at face value.

objectives.text: Apply the Nutrition Care Process to complete a comprehensive nutrition assessment including diet history, anthropometrics, labs, and psychosocial/behavioral barriers.
Formulate an accurate PES statement linking nutrition diagnosis, etiology, and signs/symptoms using assessment data.
Develop evidence-based, patient-centered nutrition interventions addressing sodium, fiber, fluid choices, and social eating patterns.
Integrate medication management considerations (GI side effects, NSAID risk, adherence) into the nutrition care plan and recognize a patient-reported vs. record-based adherence mismatch.
Apply motivational interviewing techniques to explore ambivalence, elicit the patient's own motivations, and assess readiness to change in a patient in precontemplation/early contemplation.
Identify lifestyle, financial, social, and health-literacy barriers to adherence and propose appropriate interprofessional/community referrals.

patient.name: Walter Greene
patient.appearance: Seated in a worn recliner in a modestly furnished living room, TV visible in the background paused mid-show. Wears a loose button-down shirt; visible fatigue in posture but alert and animated when talking. Keeps a cane within reach.

persona.personality: Cynical, sarcastic, fiercely independent, but warm and funny underneath once trust is built. Takes pride in his decades of work and self-reliance.
persona.communicationStyle: Direct, dismissive and testing at first ('you look like a kid'); dominates conversation with tangents about his health history or old job stories; opens up with concrete fears when met with empathy rather than pity.
persona.emotionalState: Guarded and irritable on the surface, masking underlying fear about hospitalization, loss of independence, and being a burden.
persona.background: Worked 34 years as a janitor at a local school district before retiring. Widowed; wife passed several years ago. Lives alone in a two-bedroom suburban apartment. Has a tight-knit 'dinner club' of retired friends he eats out with twice a week, and keeps in touch with old coworkers mostly online. Sister lives across the country and calls to check on him, which stirs up guilt.
speechExamples: You look like you're still in school. No offense.
Food's supposed to make you feel good, not be a chore.
I don't want to go back to that hospital. That's really all I care about.
I know I should eat better, but who's it gonna help at this point?
I don't need somebody telling me what to do like I'm a kid.
concerns: Will I have to give up eating with my friends?
Why do these pills make me feel so lousy?
Is losing this weight a bad thing or a good thing?
Are you going to make me eat like I'm in some hospital ward?
Why does everyone think I can't take care of myself?

scenario.studentBrief: You are a dietetics student conducting a telehealth nutrition assessment and counseling visit with Walter Greene, a 72-year-old man referred by his PCP for medical nutrition therapy. He has a history of Type 2 Diabetes, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, hypertension, CKD stage 3, and CAD. He has been referred for support with dietary management. Conduct a full nutrition assessment, identify barriers, and begin patient-centered counseling using motivational interviewing. Do not assume he will be receptive right away.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Referral for medical nutrition therapy due to uncontrolled Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus and heart failure with reported dietary nonadherence
scenario.openingLine: Doc sent me here. Said I need to talk to somebody about my eating. I don't really see the point, but here I am.
tasks: Complete a diet history and nutrition-focused assessment including anthropometrics, labs, and meal pattern
Explore barriers to adherence (financial, social, physiological, health literacy) using open-ended, non-judgmental questions
Review the medication list with the patient
Formulate a PES statement and begin negotiating one or two small, patient-chosen behavior changes using motivational interviewing
Discuss appropriate interprofessional referrals (e.g., diabetes education, social work, PT) and close the visit with a collaborative plan

profile.setting: Telehealth video visit; patient at home in his living room recliner, Suburban two-bedroom apartment
profile.summary: Walter Greene is a 72-year-old widowed retired janitor with uncontrolled T2DM (HbA1c 8.7%), HFrEF (EF 40%), CKD stage 3, HTN, and CAD who is referred for medical nutrition therapy after repeated hospitalizations and reported dietary nonadherence. The case challenges dietetics students to perform a full nutrition assessment via telehealth, uncover a mismatch between his self-reported medication adherence and his pharmacy refill record, and apply motivational interviewing with a guarded, humor-masking patient in precontemplation to begin negotiating sustainable, culturally respectful dietary changes.
profile.title: Uncontrolled Type 2 Diabetes and Heart Failure in a 72-Year-Old Man with Dietary Nonadherence: A Motivational Interviewing Challenge
